intro: This guide walks a Sunday school class, homeschool group or family through “The Story of Amanda Smith (For Children)” in twelve weeks, one chapter a week. It tells the true story of Amanda Berry Smith, born into slavery in Maryland, set free by her father’s hard work, who learned to trust God for everything and carried the good news of Jesus to England, India and Africa. It is written for children aged 6 to 12 and works for a family around the table or a class of up to twenty.

Each session takes about 30 minutes. Welcome everyone and say the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter aloud (5–7 minutes). Talk together using the chapter’s three questions (5–10 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Close by praying the chapter’s prayer, or your own (2 minutes).

To prepare, read the chapter yourself beforehand and have paper, pencils and crayons ready. The first chapters tell of slavery, people escaping from it, and Black children being treated unfairly at school, so speak about these things calmly and truthfully: say plainly that slavery and racism were wrong and that God made every person to be loved and free. Never act out slavery, capture or unkind treatment in a game or role-play, never single out any child because of their background, and never ask children to share their own experiences of unfairness in front of the group; keep coming back to the book’s own point, that God was with Amanda and her family all along.

weeks.summary: Amanda is born in Maryland in the days when Black families like hers were not free and were made to work without pay. Her father, Samuel Berry, works for his owner all day and then makes brooms, weaves corn-husk mats, burns lime and works in the fields far into the night, saving penny by penny until he has bought his own freedom, then his wife’s, then each of his children’s, Amanda’s too. Explain slavery simply and truthfully as something deeply wrong, without adding detail beyond the chapter, and do not act any of it out. The big idea: Amanda’s father worked hard to set his family free, and our heavenly Father gave his own Son, Jesus, to set us free as a gift.

memory_verse.text: If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.

activity.title: A Thank-You for Hard Work
steps: Fold a sheet of paper in half to make a card.
On the front, draw a grown-up who works hard to look after you, doing one of their jobs.
Inside, write “Thank you for loving me” and sign your name.
Under that, write or draw “Jesus is God’s gift to me,” and take the card home to give away.

weeks.summary: Amanda’s grandmother loves God and prays for years that her grandchildren will be free, slipping out into the bushes to “tell Jesus” whatever is too big to carry. A young woman named Miss Celie gives her heart to Jesus at a camp meeting, and when she falls ill and is dying she asks her family three times to let Samuel buy his wife and children, until they promise. Each time, Grandmother hurries out to thank God. Mention Miss Celie’s death simply, as the chapter does. The big idea: keep on praying, even when the answer takes a long time, because God hears every word.

activity.title: My Keep-Praying Chart
steps: Fold a sheet of paper in half, then in half again, then in half once more, and open it out to show eight boxes.
In the first box, draw or write one thing you want to keep praying for. It can stay private.
Write the days of the week in the other seven boxes.
Take your chart home and tick a box each day you “tell Jesus” about it, as Amanda’s grandmother did.

weeks.summary: Now free and living on a farm in Pennsylvania, the Berry family’s house becomes a secret safe place where Samuel helps tired, frightened people who have run away from slavery travel on to freedom. One morning four men ride up to search the house, and Amanda’s mother quickly hides an escaped man beneath the mattress and lays her sleeping two-year-old on top; the men search everywhere but never find him. Do not turn this story into a hiding or chasing game; keep the focus on the family’s courage and kindness. The big idea: when God gives us a chance to help someone in trouble, we can be brave and kind.

memory_verse.text: For I was hungry, and you gave me food to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you took me in.

activity.title: A House with the Light On
steps: Draw a little farmhouse with one window glowing bright yellow, like a light left on for someone who needs help.
Around the house, draw a garden path leading to the door.
Along the path, draw or write ways you can be a safe and gentle friend, like sharing, listening or standing up for someone.
Write “I was a stranger, and you took me in” across the top and take it home.

weeks.summary: Amanda longs to go to school, but Black children are hardly allowed to learn and she is made to wait at the back while the others are taught first; in all her life she has only about three months of school. One freezing morning she walks two and a half miles through deep snow and arrives too cold to speak. At home she cuts big letters from her father’s newspapers, lines them up on the windowsill, and with her mother’s help reads her first sentence: “The house, the tree, the dog, the cow.” Say plainly that treating Amanda this way was wrong, and do not ask children to act out or tell about being treated unfairly. The big idea: learning is a gift from God, and a patient heart that keeps trying can do wonderful things.

memory_verse.text: Wisdom is supreme. Get wisdom. Yes, though it costs all your possessions, get understanding.

activity.title: The Windowsill Sentence
activity.materials: Sheets of paper and a thick crayon (the leader writes one big letter on each sheet beforehand)
steps: Before the session, write big letters on separate sheets of paper: T, H, E, D, O, G, C, W, R, A, S and a few extra vowels.
Give each child one or two letters to hold up.
Call out a short word from Amanda’s first sentence, like “the,” “dog” or “cow,” and let the children with those letters stand in a line to spell it.
Try new words together, then say Amanda’s whole sentence out loud: “The house, the tree, the dog, the cow.”

weeks.summary: Grown-up Amanda wants to belong to God, but her strong will wants to be saved her own quiet way, and a whispering voice tells her God will not hear her. One afternoon, working in a kind Quaker family’s home, she goes down to the cellar to pray and says, “O Lord, if Thou wilt help me, I will believe Thee,” and the moment she trusts him, joy floods her soul and her burden rolls away. The big idea: we do not have to make ourselves good enough first; Jesus welcomes anyone who simply comes to him and trusts him.

memory_verse.text: All that which the Father gives me will come to me. Him who comes to me I will in no way throw out.

activity.title: Look in the Mirror
steps: Draw a big oval mirror with a fancy frame around it.
Inside the mirror, draw your own face with a big, happy smile, the way Amanda looked in the mirror after she trusted Jesus.
Around the frame, write “Jesus welcomes me just as I am.”
Hold up your mirrors and say the memory verse together.

weeks.summary: Amanda borrows fifty dollars to help set her younger sister Frances free, and the debt worries her day and night. When she finds three hundred dollars that a visitor, Mr. Robert, dropped on the kitchen floor, a sneaky thought tells her to keep it, but she says no and hands back every dollar. Mr. Robert is so grateful that he gives her fifty dollars, exactly what she needs. The big idea: be honest even when no one is watching, because God sees and takes care of us.

memory_verse.text: He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is unrighteous in a very little is also unrighteous in much.

activity.title: Honest or Not?
steps: Teach the signs: thumbs up for “That’s honest,” thumbs down for “That’s not honest.”
Read out simple made-up situations, such as finding a coin on the floor at a friend’s house, being given too much change, or seeing that a classmate dropped a pencil.
For each one, let everyone show a thumb, then ask one child what the honest thing to do would be.
Finish by saying together, “Honest when no one is looking,” and praying for courage to do the right thing.

weeks.summary: One Sunday Amanda leaves baby Will asleep in his cradle with her older daughter Mazie and goes to hear a preacher, but in church frightening thoughts tell her the baby has been dropped and she must run home. Remembering she has told others to trust God, she says, “I will trust the Lord, even with my baby,” stays, and is filled with peace; at home she finds Will sleeping sweetly, never having woken. Reassure any anxious child that the baby was perfectly safe. The big idea: when scary “what ifs” fill our minds, we can give the worry to God and trust him.

memory_verse.text: When I am afraid, I will put my trust in you.

activity.title: What If? I Will Trust!
steps: Stand in a circle and teach the reply: hands on heart and say, “When I am afraid, I will trust in God!”
The leader calls out an everyday “what if,” such as “What if it thunders tonight?” or “What if I get lost in the shop?”
After each one, everyone gives the reply together and then takes one slow, calm breath.
Let children who would like to call out a “what if” of their own, then end with the memory verse in a whisper.

weeks.summary: Amanda feels sure God wants her to go and tell people about Jesus in Salem, a far-off town where she knows no one, but her shoes have holes worn through and she has no money for new ones. She prays, “Lord, if it is Your will, please give me the money for shoes,” and a few days later Father Brummell quietly presses something into her hand as he says goodbye; by the fire that night she counts five dollars, exactly enough. The big idea: God is never too busy for the small things we need, so we can tell him about everything and trust him for the answer.

memory_verse.text: My God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.

activity.title: My Prayer Shoe
steps: Stand with one foot, shoe on, on a sheet of paper and have a friend draw around your shoe.
Colour in your shoe and give it laces, buckles or stripes.
Inside the shoe, write or draw one small thing you need that you can tell God about.
Pray together, “Thank you, God, that you care about the little things,” and take your shoe home.

weeks.summary: Friends tell Amanda they believe God wants her to sail to England to tell people about Jesus, but she is secretly afraid of the deep sea and even writes a letter saying she will not go. That evening a heavy sadness comes over her, and as she kneels God gently shows her she has been telling others to trust him in the dark while refusing to do it herself; she asks forgiveness, goes, and God goes with her all the way. The big idea: it is easier to tell others to be brave than to be brave ourselves, but God goes with us through the deep water.

memory_verse.text: When you pass through the waters, I will be with you.

activity.title: Through the Deep Water
activity.materials: Nothing (a clear space in the room)
steps: Choose one side of the room as America and the other side as England, with the “ocean” in between.
Everyone begins in America; the leader calls out how to cross: tiptoe, giant steps, swimming arms or rocking like a ship.
Each time the group reaches the other side, everyone calls out together, “God was with me all the way!”
Cross back and forth a few times, then sit down and say the first line of the memory verse together.

weeks.summary: On the ship to Africa, men break the lock on Amanda’s trunk and steal many of her things, even her shoes, and some she never gets back. The captain is amazed that she keeps her temper, and Amanda tells him that if getting angry would bring her things back he would see her carry on, but since it would not, why should she; God keeps her heart quiet and calm. The big idea: anger does not fix what goes wrong, but God can help us stay calm and gentle, and that is real strength.

memory_verse.text: One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty; one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city.

activity.title: Calm Like Amanda
steps: Teach a calm-down breath: breathe in slowly as if smelling a flower, then breathe out slowly as if blowing out a candle.
The leader names something frustrating, such as a toy breaking, a tower knocked over or losing a game.
For each one, everyone first shows a cross face for one second, then does three flower-and-candle breaths together.
After the breaths, ask the group what a calm and gentle thing to do next would be, and finish by praying, “God, rule my heart with your peace.”

weeks.summary: In India, Amanda and her friend Miss Frow are riding in a bullock cart on a dark country road when the bullocks stop and will not take another step. Climbing down, the two women walk a few steps ahead and find a deep ditch cut across the whole road; if the animals had gone on, the cart would have crashed. The big idea: God sometimes protects us in ways we cannot see, and a “no” or a delay can really be him keeping us safe.

memory_verse.text: For he will give his angels charge over you, to guard you in all your ways.

activity.title: Lead Me Safely
activity.materials: A few chairs or cushions to walk around
steps: Set out a few chairs or cushions as gentle obstacles in an open space.
In pairs, one child closes their eyes while the other holds their hand and guides them slowly around the obstacles, saying “Stop!” and “Go on” when needed.
Walk only, never run, and swap places after one trip.
Sit together and talk about how it felt to trust someone who could see what you could not, then say the memory verse.

weeks.summary: Living in Africa, Amanda grows to love two little boys who visit her, especially bright-smiling Bob, whose father, Jack, asks her to take his son and teach him about God, because he himself never learned. Amanda is often ill and has little money, but in prayer God tells her, “You do what you can, and where you leave off, God will raise up somebody else to do the rest,” so she takes Bob as her very own boy. The big idea: God does not ask us to do everything ourselves, only what we can, trusting him with the rest; and welcoming a child is like welcoming Jesus.

memory_verse.text: Whoever will receive one such little child in my name receives me.

activity.title: Do What You Can
activity.materials: One large sheet of paper and crayons
steps: Put one big sheet of paper in the middle and tell the children you will draw a picture of a happy home together.
Each child adds one thing, such as a roof, a door, a tree, a sun or a person, then passes the crayon on to the next child.
Keep going until everyone has had a turn and the picture is finished.
Look at it together and talk about how no one did it all, but everyone did what they could, just as God told Amanda.
